lead: A phone upload or a camera feed produces media faster than any person can watch it. So social networks and surveillance systems both turn media into a machine-readable record: detect, describe, index, store, act. The stages are the same; the goal differs. One ranks posts for attention, the other raises alerts for safety. Only a few universities teach this material, and it is the practical face of multimedia big data.
prereq: You need: 6.3 for feature vectors kept beside metadata, and 6.6 for segmentation and buffering.

blocks.text: An upload lands unchanged in object storage. A worker then builds a transcoding ladder: the same clip re-encoded at 240p, 480p, 720p and 1080p and cut into short segments. A phone on a weak link starts at the bottom rung and climbs, as in 6.6.

Duplicate and copyright checks use a perceptual hash: a short fingerprint that barely changes after resizing, re-compression or a small crop. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 flips completely on one bit, so it can never match a re-encoded copy. Two perceptual fingerprints within a small distance are declared the same media.

Tagging adds text: captions, speech-to-text transcripts, classifier labels. Those labels and the fingerprint become a feature vector stored beside the row (6.3). Ranking then scores candidate posts for one user by predicted engagement, freshness and similarity to past viewing, and returns the top few.

Most surveillance frames are empty. A motion gate compares each frame with a background model and drops frames that differ little. On a quiet corridor at night this one step cuts detection compute by an order of magnitude.

Detection finds people and vehicles in the surviving frames; tracking gives each one a stable id. The metadata stage writes a small row per event: timestamp, camera id, site, object class, bounding box, track id and a perceptual hash of the frame. Video goes to storage; the row goes to an index.

Storage is tiered: recent footage on fast disk for a week or two, older footage on cheap object storage or deleted. A retention policy fixes the days per tier, often 7 hot and 30 cold. A search such as "red truck, gate 3, after 21:00" is answered from the index without decoding video. Alerts fire on rules or on classifier scores. Consent and purpose limitation are legal duties, not features.

blocks.where: R is the recording bit rate in bit/s; 86,400 is the number of seconds in one day; dividing by 8 converts bits to bytes; dividing by 10⁹ gives GB.

figure.caption: Stored data grows in a straight line with the number of days kept. After 30 days of retention, 64 cameras at 4 Mbit/s need 82.9 TB if recorded around the clock, but 16.6 TB when the motion gate makes recording happen for only 20% of the day — about one fifth.

spec.aria: A line graph of stored terabytes against retention days from 0 to 30. The upper line, 24-hour recording, rises to 82.9 terabytes at day 30; the lower line, motion-gated recording at 20 percent, rises to 16.6 terabytes.

examples.question: A campus runs 64 cameras at 1080p, each producing 4 Mbit/s, recorded 24 hours a day with 30 days of retention. Find the storage per camera per day, for all cameras per day, and for the full retention period.
steps: Bits per camera per day = 4 × 10⁶ bit/s × 86,400 s = 3.456 × 10¹¹ bit.
Bytes per camera per day = 3.456 × 10¹¹ ÷ 8 = 4.32 × 10¹⁰ B = 43.2 GB.
All cameras per day = 64 × 43.2 GB = 2764.8 GB ≈ 2.76 TB.
examples.answer: 43.2 GB per camera per day, about 2.76 TB per day for the campus, and about 82.9 TB for 30 days.
examples.check:
R = 4e6
secs = 86400
N = 64
D = 30
per_cam_day = R * secs / 8 / 1e9
print(round(per_cam_day, 1))
print(round(N * per_cam_day, 1))
print(round(N * per_cam_day * D / 1000, 1))

examples.question: The same campus enables motion-gated recording, so it records only 20% of each day. What is the 30-day total now?
steps: Per camera per day = 43.2 GB × 0.2 = 8.64 GB.
All cameras per day = 64 × 8.64 GB = 552.96 GB.
examples.answer: About 16.6 TB, roughly one fifth of the continuous figure.

traps: Forgetting to multiply by the number of cameras: 43.2 GB is one camera, not the campus.
Mixing Mbit/s with MB/s. 4 Mbit/s records 43.2 GB per day, not 345.6 GB.
Using 86,400 s correctly but then forgetting the 30 days, or using 3600 s per day by mistake.
Confusing the perceptual hash with a cryptographic hash. One must survive re-encoding; the other must not.
Assuming a motion gate shrinks storage. It shrinks compute; storage drops only if the recording policy itself becomes event-only.

quiz.q: State the purpose of a perceptual hash.
quiz.a: It gives a short fingerprint that stays nearly the same after resizing, re-compression or cropping, so near-duplicate media can be matched.

quiz.q: Why does a transcoding ladder help a phone on a weak link?
quiz.a: The clip exists at several bitrates as segments, so the client starts at a low rung it can sustain and moves up when bandwidth allows.

quiz.q: 20 cameras at 2 Mbit/s, 24 hours a day, 14 days retention. Find the total storage.
quiz.a: Per camera per day = 2 × 10⁶ × 86,400 ÷ 8 ÷ 10⁹ = 21.6 GB. All cameras per day = 432 GB. Fourteen days = 6048 GB ≈ 6.05 TB.

quiz.q: A motion gate cuts detection work by 80% but storage stays the same. Explain.
quiz.a: The gate skips frames before detection, saving compute. Recording still covers 24 hours at a fixed bit rate, and storage depends on bit rate × time, not on how many frames were analysed.

quiz.q: Why tier surveillance storage into hot and cold?
quiz.a: Recent footage is searched often and must answer in seconds, so it sits on fast disks. Older footage is rarely touched, so cheap object storage or deletion is enough.

quiz.q: A 2-hour 1080p clip at 4 Mbit/s is stored. How large is it?

beyond: Not for the exam. Real deployments push the metadata stage into the camera or an edge box, so only events and hashes travel to the cloud; this is the edge-cloud split you will meet in IoT courses. Similarity search now runs on learned embeddings rather than hand-built features, and vector indexes answer a query over millions of clips. Search terms: perceptual hashing, video content analysis, retention policy, edge inference, vector database.
